SK4034 The collection is sorted before it is filtered

xs.OrderBy(k).Where(p) buffers, keys and sorts every element, and then throws some of them away; xs.Where(p).OrderBy(k) does all three to the survivors only.

CategoryPerformance
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS6607

Why

OrderBy is not lazy in the way the rest of the pipeline is: it buffers the entire sequence, computes a key for every element and sorts all of them before it yields the first one. Putting Where after it means paying O(n log n) on elements that are about to be discarded, and holding a buffer and a key array sized to the input rather than to the output. Swapping the two makes every one of those proportional to what survives — the one rewrite in this range that moves an asymptotic term rather than an allocation count.

Example

Instead of:

var recent = entries.OrderBy(entry => entry.Created).Where(entry => entry.IsVisible);

Write:

var recent = entries.Where(entry => entry.IsVisible).OrderBy(entry => entry.Created);

When it does not fire

⚠ The output sequence is identical, and that rests entirely on `OrderBy` being a stable sort. A stable sort leaves elements with equal keys in their original relative order and Where preserves relative order, so both spellings emit the survivors ordered by key with ties broken by source position. LINQ documents OrderBy as stable; were it not, the two orders would differ for equal keys and this rule would be wrong. ⚠ The indexed `Where(Func<T, int, bool>)` overload is refused. After the sort the index is a position in sorted order and before it a position in source order, so moving that call rewrites the program rather than the pipeline. A parameter count alone would not tell the two overloads apart — the predicate's shape is what does. ⚠ Queryable is excluded for the reason SK4010 excludes it: a provider is free to translate one ordering of a pipeline and not the other, and a fix that turns a working query into a runtime "unsupported expression" is worse than the sort it saved. ⚠ What does change is when the two functions run and on what. The predicate is now invoked in source order rather than in sorted order, and the key selector runs only on the survivors — so a key selector that throws for an element the filter would have removed used to throw and now does not, and a predicate with side effects observes a different order. Both are defects in the lambda rather than in the rewrite, and neither is decidable without proving a lambda pure. ⚠ The static type of the whole expression widens from `IEnumerable<T>` to `IOrderedEnumerable<T>`. Every context that accepted the first accepts the second, but a var declaration now infers the ordered type and an overload set containing both could resolve differently. ⚠ Where the Where is immediately consumed by one of SK4010's nine operators, this rule says nothing: both are right about xs.OrderBy(k).Where(p).First() and their edits overlap, so SK4010 keeps it — folding the predicate into First lets the search stop at the first match, and once applied this shape no longer exists. ⚠ A ThenBy between the two calls is not this shape and is not reported, because the Where receiver is then the ThenBy rather than the sort.
